ballot.name: Article 14 (CRA Exploit Clock)
ballot.promise: The moment a component you ship is confirmed actively exploited, your EU Cyber Resilience Act 24-hour report is already drafted and your clock is already running.
ballot.synthesis: Watches every shipped version’s SBOM against CISA KEV, OSV and GHSA on an hourly cron; when an exploited component matches, starts the CRA Article 14 24-hour early-warning clock and generates the ENISA-format notification draft plus the dated evidence trail. Hard external trigger: CRA reporting obligations begin 11 September 2026 — 23 days from today. Run-2 heritage: this idea (merged with Noticeboard as “Ship Record”) placed 2nd of 8 in run-2’s Borda vote; the licence/NOTICE half stays as an expansion tier, the CRA clock leads.
ballot.buyer: EU-selling software/device vendors’ engineering leads; the long tail below FOSSA/enterprise GRC.

underlying.name: Article14
underlying.one_liner: Watches the SBOM of every version you have shipped against CISA KEV, OSV and GHSA hourly, and the moment a component you ship is confirmed actively exploited it starts the EU Cyber Resilience Act 24-hour clock and generates the ENISA early-warning and 72-hour notification drafts with the full evidence chain.
underlying.problem: From 11 September 2026 — four weeks from today — every manufacturer placing products with digital elements on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities to ENISA and the coordinating CSIRT within 24 hours, with a full notification at 72 hours. This is confirmed on the European Commission's own CRA page (entry into force 10 Dec 2024, reporting obligations 11 Sep 2026, full application 11 Dec 2027). Scope includes software shipped before the date. Penalties run to EUR 15M or 2.5% of worldwide turnover. The structural problem is that you cannot report what you cannot see: SBOM obligations are not formally enforceable until Dec 2027, which creates an implicit 15-month-early SBOM deadline — a 24-hour clock leaves no room for manual component archaeology. Small vendors have no per-release SBOM and no automated exploit watch. The incumbents are enterprise and sales-led; the one self-serve option found, sbomify, is $159/mo and is an artifact hub, not a clock.
underlying.target_customer: 10–200 person software, IoT, embedded and devtool vendors that sell into the EU and have no dedicated security team. Buyer is the CTO or head of engineering who has just been sent the CRA question by a customer or a board member. Christensen JTBD: the job is 'let me be able to answer the 24-hour clock without hiring anyone', not 'give me a vulnerability scanner'.
underlying.revenue_model: Subscription tiered by number of products and released versions under continuous watch, billed monthly via Stripe with automated dunning; annual prepay at -20%. Natural expansion axis is versions-under-watch, which grows every release, so revenue compounds with the customer's own shipping cadence without any human touch.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: $99/mo Solo (1 product, 25 shipped versions, KEV/OSV watch, alerts) → $299/mo Team (5 products, 250 versions, ENISA 24h/72h draft generator, PagerDuty/webhook, signed immutable attestation log) → $799/mo Fleet (unlimited, customer-facing SBOM distribution portal, VEX publishing). Anchored against a EUR 15M downside and against sbomify's $159 self-serve tier. Ramanujam: willingness to pay here is driven by the deadline, not by feature count, so the packaging boundary is 'does it produce the filing artifact', which is exactly where the value step is.
underlying.knowledge_base: Three layers. (1) A per-release SBOM store: every version you ever shipped, in CycloneDX 1.6 / SPDX 3.0.1, built in your CI and stored immutably with artifact hashes — this is the asset a competitor cannot recreate for you retroactively and it is the reason the product is sticky. (2) The exploitation corpus: CISA KEV JSON feed, OSV.dev v1 API (verified live and free, returns id/aliases/affected package ranges/severity/references), GitHub GHSA, EPSS daily scores, NVD. (3) A CRA obligation model we maintain: which Art. 14 / Annex I duties attach to which event class, the 24h / 72h / 14-day decision trees, and the ENISA Single Reporting Platform field schema. Refresh crons: KEV and EPSS daily 04:00 UTC; OSV and GHSA hourly deltas; EU and ENISA guidance pages weekly with a diff alert into the obligation model's changelog. Staleness detection: if KEV has not refreshed in 36 h the product shows a red 'exploit feed stale since <timestamp>' banner and degrades to OSV-only mode with explicitly narrowed claims.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App plus Stripe Checkout; the first SBOM lands within one CI run, no demo. A2: SBOM generation, component matching, clock arithmetic and draft assembly are all code; the LLM writes only the narrative fields of the notification from a fixed template with the facts injected, then a validator checks every required ENISA field is present. A3: a fuzzy component-name match to a KEV entry is never clock-starting — it surfaces as 'Possible match, not clock-starting' with both records side by side and a one-click 'this is / is not my component' that writes to the customer's own VEX suppression list, narrowing future claims. The product states plainly and permanently in-product that it detects and drafts but does not file and is not legal advice. No queue, no expert, no escalation. A4: KEV, OSV, GHSA, EPSS and the EU/ENISA pages are all public and machine-readable, on the crons above. A5: CI-triggered plus scheduled; if SBOM generation fails for a release, the last good SBOM stays authoritative and the customer is told loudly that the new version is UNWATCHED — fail closed and visible, never silently green. A6: zero human minutes; the support surface is a deterministic in-product scope decision tree citing the regulation.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: 3–5 weeks, and it is the most time-critical idea in this set. Launching in the last week of August 2026 lands directly on the 11 September 2026 obligation date. Blank's customer-development loop can run against a live deadline instead of a hypothetical, and the landing page can be a free deterministic 'are you in CRA scope' checker that captures email and converts.
underlying.risks: Scope confusion is the biggest conversion blocker — many buyers genuinely do not know if they are in scope, so the free scope checker must be deterministic and citation-backed or it becomes an advice product. Regulator guidance will move between now and Dec 2027, so the obligation model must be versioned and the guidance pages diffed weekly. Snyk, Mend and Sonatype could bundle a CRA clock and give it away; the defence is self-serve pricing and the per-release SBOM archive, not features. Compliance-theatre perception is real — the product must be honest that it is a detection and drafting engine. And the hard line: it must never claim to file on the customer's behalf, which caps the promise but keeps A2/A3 clean. HN sentiment on the CRA is politically hostile (eight stories, up to 215 points, largely about open-source burden), so messaging must be operational, not celebratory.

underlying.name: Noticeboard
underlying.one_liner: Generates the legally-correct attribution/NOTICE artifact for every release you cut, and watches your whole dependency tree for licence changes — the Redis, HashiCorp and Elastic style rug-pulls — before they land in your build.
underlying.problem: Two boring, recurring, well-specified obligations that almost nobody automates. First, everything you ship that leaves your servers owes attribution: MIT, BSD and Apache all require notice, copyleft requires more, and most small teams ship nothing or a stale hand-maintained file — until an enterprise customer's legal review asks for the attribution document and the deal stalls. Second, licences change underneath you: Redis moved from BSD-3 to RSALv2/SSPL at version 7.4 (announced March 2024, non-retroactive), Terraform moved MPL 2.0 to BSL in August 2023, Elasticsearch to SSPL in January 2021. Socket's writeup records the downstream consequence — Redis 'is being actively pinned to older versions, or just outright removed from repositories, linux distributions'. Nobody reads the LICENSE file of 1,400 transitive dependencies on a schedule. The source of truth is fully public and machine-readable: the SPDX License List is at v3.28.0 dated 2026-02-20 with per-licence JSON in the spdx/license-list-data repo, versioned and rebuilt on every release. FOSSA occupies the top of this market at $20/project/month (their own example works out to $207/mo for ten projects) with an enterprise motion above it; the SMB self-serve tier is thin and does not include a relicensing watch.
underlying.target_customer: 3–50 engineer teams shipping software that leaves their infrastructure — desktop and mobile apps, containers, on-prem installs, SDKs, firmware — plus any SaaS that has to survive enterprise legal review. Buyer is the founding engineer or eng lead who just got the attribution request in a procurement thread.
underlying.revenue_model: Subscription tiered by repo count, with the per-release attribution artifact as the unit of value. Stripe Checkout and Billing, automated dunning, annual at -20%. Expansion is repo count plus the hosted public attribution page, which becomes a link on the customer's own site and is therefore very hard to churn out of.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: $39/mo Indie (3 repos, NOTICE per release, relicensing watch) → $119/mo Team (15 repos, CI policy gate, copyleft linkage analysis, dated archive) → $349/mo Business (unlimited repos, SPDX/CycloneDX export, self-hosted runner, customer-facing attribution page on your domain). Priced under FOSSA's effective per-project rate at the low end so the comparison is trivially favourable, then differentiated upward on the relicensing watch, which FOSSA does not sell as a product. Hormozi: the offer is 'never be the reason the deal stalls in legal', bundled with 'never be surprised by a rug-pull'.
underlying.knowledge_base: Three layers, one of which is a genuine time-moat. (1) The SPDX License List, machine-readable JSON, one file per licence and exception, versioned vX.Y.Z tracking the list release — pure ingestion. (2) The obligation matrix, which we author and maintain: per SPDX ID x distribution mode (SaaS / binary / container / statically linked / dynamically linked / modified source) which obligations trigger — attribution text, licence copy, written source offer, modification statement, patent grant, network-use trigger, notice placement. SPDX gives you the licence identity for free; nobody gives you the obligation encoding, and that is the product. (3) The relicensing event history: per package, dated snapshots of the declared licence across every published version, built by walking registry metadata and repo LICENSE file hashes. You cannot retro-acquire 'what did this package's licence say on this date' once you start late — we begin accumulating on day one and backfill from registry history. Refresh crons: SPDX release watch daily; registry metadata plus LICENSE hash for the union of all customers' dependency trees nightly 02:00 UTC; a licence-change event fires within 24 h of publication. Staleness: each registry's last successful crawl timestamp is shown in-product, and a stale registry marks its packages 'last verified <date>' rather than asserting current state.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: GitHub App plus Stripe Checkout, first NOTICE artifact generated within minutes of install. A2: licence detection is deterministic — text hashing and template matching against the SPDX licence texts — and NOTICE assembly is templated from the obligation matrix; the LLM is used only to summarise an unrecognised licence text into the obligation schema, and its output is always displayed alongside the raw text. A3: when a licence cannot be identified with high confidence the component goes into a visible 'Unresolved — N components' bucket, is excluded from any completeness claim, and the emitted artifact carries an explicit dated caveat listing them. The product refuses to stamp a clean bill it cannot support. The in-product resolve flow lets the customer paste the licence text for exact matching — still no human of ours in the loop, and no legal advice is ever offered, only obligations with citations. A4: SPDX and the package registries are public and machine-readable, on the crons above. A5: nightly crons; a failed registry crawl leaves yesterday's snapshot standing and the UI says so — fail closed. A6: zero human minutes; the support surface is the obligation matrix itself, published and browsable.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: 4–6 weeks. Wedge and single Bullseye channel: a free 'what should be in your NOTICE file' scanner for any public GitHub repo, which is SEO-native, shareable, and produces the exact artifact the buyer will later need for a real release. Fitzpatrick's Mom Test applies to validation here — ask what they sent the last time legal asked, not whether they would buy this.
underlying.risks: Latent pain: buyers do not feel attribution until legal asks, so the relicensing watch has to carry the urgency — the Redis and HashiCorp events are memorable and recent enough to do that work. The output must never read as legal advice; it states obligations with citations and nothing more, which is both a legal safety rule and an A3 constraint. FOSSA or Snyk could compress their SMB tier and squeeze the price. Detection has real false negatives on vendored, minified or dual-licensed code, so the Unresolved bucket must be prominent rather than hidden or the whole trust model collapses. Finally, relicensing events are rare — perhaps a handful of consequential ones a year — so the watch is insurance, and insurance churns unless the NOTICE artifact carries the day-to-day value.

ballot.name: ExclusionAuto
ballot.promise: Flat-fee, unlimited-roster monthly OIG-LEIE + SAM.gov exclusion re-screening — the per-screen caps and custom-quote walls of incumbents, deleted.
ballot.synthesis: Monthly re-screen of an uploaded staff/vendor roster against the two federal machine-readable exclusion feeds (OIG LEIE CSV, monthly by the 10th; SAM.gov exclusions API, daily incrementals), with dated evidence PDFs per screen cycle. Name-match ambiguity degrades in-product (shows the candidate rows and match score; never asserts identity). Expansion: PECOS revalidation due-date monitoring from CMS’s monthly file (see r3 raw-ideas “PECOS Sentinel”).
ballot.buyer: Small practices, home-health and healthcare staffing agencies with turnover-heavy rosters of 100+ names; the exact segment incumbent per-screen caps push into custom quotes.

underlying.name: ExclusionAuto
underlying.one_liner: Flat-fee, unlimited-roster monthly OIG-LEIE + SAM.gov exclusion re-screening for small practices, home-health and staffing agencies, fully self-serve against the two federal machine-readable exclusion feeds.
underlying.problem: HHS-OIG requires providers to screen every employee and vendor against the federal exclusion lists, ideally monthly, because billing for services rendered even indirectly by an excluded individual creates civil monetary penalty exposure; small practices and staffing agencies with large hourly-worker rosters are the ones least equipped to do this by hand.
underlying.target_customer: Small physician practices, home-health/staffing agencies, and DME suppliers with rosters too large for manual monthly LEIE lookups but too small to negotiate an enterprise compliance contract.
underlying.evidence: A direct self-serve competitor already sells this: ExclusionScreening.com's published pricing shows Basic from $30/mo and Premium from $40/mo, with the Premium tier capped at 'up to 100 screens per month' covering OIG LEIE, GSA SAM, and the 46 state Medicaid exclusion lists, with 'custom pricing' gating anyone above that volume (https://exclusionscreening.com/pricing/, fetched via search 2026-08-19). That per-screen cap is exactly the gap a flat-fee, unlimited-roster automated re-screen can undercut for staffing agencies with turnover-heavy rosters of 200+ workers.
underlying.knowledge_base: Two federal, directly-fetched, machine-readable feeds: (1) HHS-OIG LEIE full database CSV at https://oig.hhs.gov/exclusions/downloadables/UPDATED.csv — fetched live 2026-08-19 (HTTP 200, 15.5MB), confirmed columns LASTNAME, FIRSTNAME, BUSNAME, NPI, EXCLTYPE, EXCLDATE, REINDATE, replaced monthly by OIG's own stated cadence ('updated by the 10th of every month', per https://oig.hhs.gov/exclusions/leie-database-supplement-downloads/); (2) GSA SAM.gov Exclusions Public Extract, a documented CSV/JSON API at https://api.sam.gov/entity-information/v4/download-exclusions (endpoint confirmed live/reachable, returns 404-without-key rather than DNS/connection failure, per GSA's own API docs at https://open.gsa.gov/api/exclusions-api/, fetched 2026-08-19), refreshed on a documented monthly-full/daily-incremental cadence per GSA's extract documentation.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, bulk roster upload (CSV or API), card payment, no sales call. A2: fulfilment is deterministic name/NPI matching against the freshly pulled LEIE and SAM CSVs, run on a schedule, producing a match/no-match report. A3: on an ambiguous name match (common surname collisions are LEIE's well-known weakness) the product flags it explicitly as 'needs manual confirmation - possible match, not certain' with the raw LEIE row shown, rather than asserting exclusion status — it degrades to showing evidence, never adjudicates. A4: LEIE re-pulled monthly per OIG's stated cadence, SAM re-pulled on GSA's documented extract schedule; staleness self-detected by comparing the file's declared update date to expected cadence. A5: ingestion, re-screening, and dunning all cron/webhook-driven, fail-closed. A6: no human review sits between roster upload and report — screening volume is unbounded by design (that's the differentiator vs. the incumbent's per-screen cap).
underlying.moat: Combining both federal feeds (many competitors emphasize LEIE alone) with unlimited, flat-fee re-screening removes the per-screen throttling that pushes larger rosters into the incumbent's opaque custom-quote tier — a structural pricing/product wedge, not just a cheaper clone.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: $49/mo flat for unlimited roster size and unlimited monthly re-screens (vs. incumbent's $40/mo capped at 100 screens/mo), positioned specifically at staffing/home-health agencies whose rosters exceed that cap.
underlying.revenue_model: Subscription SaaS, flat monthly fee, Stripe billing, annual discount.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: 2-3 weeks: this is the simplest of the three builds (two CSV feeds, one fuzzy-match engine, one report generator).
underlying.risks: This is the most competitively crowded of the three (ExclusionScreening.com, ProviderTrust, Verisys already operate here), so differentiation must hold on the uncapped-roster/self-serve-signup wedge rather than novelty of data access; name-matching false positives/negatives on a common-name file like LEIE are an inherent, disclosed limitation rather than a data-freshness problem.
underlying.why_simple: Pure deterministic string/ID matching against two well-documented federal CSV feeds — no generative or judgment component in the fulfilment path.

underlying.name: PECOS Sentinel
underlying.one_liner: Automated Medicare revalidation & PECOS-deactivation deadline monitor for billing companies and group practices, built directly on CMS's own monthly revalidation feed.
underlying.problem: Every enrolled Medicare provider/supplier must revalidate on a CMS-set cycle (roughly every 3-5 years); MACs mail/portal notices 90-120 days out, and if the notice is missed the provider's billing privileges are deactivated with NO retroactive billing for the gap. Real practice reports: 'a revalidation notice had gone to a suite they left two years ago... they found out they were deactivated from a zero-dollar remittance, not a warning' and 'even a few weeks of lost billing can mean tens of thousands of dollars' (https://staffingly.com/insights/pain-points-solutions/medicare-deactivated-us-over-a-revalidation-notice-we-never-saw/, fetched via search 2026-08-19). Existing paid fixes are manual: credentialing firms charge ~$780 per individual revalidation (https://wchsb.com/services/credentialing-prices/) and $600-2,400/provider/year in ongoing credentialing maintenance (https://maverickhealthinnovations.com/blog/medical-credentialing-cost/), both fetched 2026-08-19.
underlying.target_customer: Medical billing / RCM companies and multi-provider group practices (5-200 NPIs) responsible for keeping their own or their clients' Medicare enrollment active.
underlying.evidence: Worse solutions already being paid for: (1) manual spreadsheet tracking, which fails as shown by the staffingly.com deactivation stories above; (2) credentialing consultancies charging $780/revalidation (WCH, fetched 2026-08-19) and $600-2,400/provider/year (Maverick Health, fetched 2026-08-19), most of which is opaque quote-based pricing rather than self-serve monitoring (https://qualigenix.com/medicare-revalidation-2026/, fetched 2026-08-19, notes most credentialing companies don't publish prices and sell via private quote).
underlying.knowledge_base: CMS 'Revalidation Due Date List' dataset, discoverable and machine-parseable via the official DCAT-US catalog at https://data.cms.gov/data.json (fetched 2026-08-19, 200 OK, 3MB JSON, 159 datasets). The dataset entry shows modified: 2026-08-05 and lists 40+ monthly CSV distributions back to 2022 (e.g. .../2026-08/1df6c395.../revalidation_base.csv, .../2026-07/..., .../2026-01/...). I directly fetched the live August-2026 file (HTTP 200, Last-Modified: Tue 04 Aug 2026) and confirmed columns: Enrollment ID, NPI, First/Last Name, Organization Name, Enrollment State Code, Provider Type Text, Enrollment Specialty, Revalidation Due Date, Adjusted Due Date, Individual Total Reassign To. Refresh cadence is monthly (verified by the run of dated directories from 2022-03 through 2026-08); staleness is self-detectable by diffing the data.json 'modified' field against an expected ~30-day cadence.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: customer signs up, uploads/syncs their NPI roster, pays via Stripe, gets a dashboard/email/SMS — no sales call or manual provisioning. A2: fulfilment is a deterministic monthly join of the customer's NPI list against the freshly pulled CMS CSV; alerts are templated, not authored. A3: when an NPI's due date is 'TBD' (outside the 6-month CMS window) or absent from the file, the product says exactly that and shows the raw CMS row plus a direct PECOS link — it never guesses a date or advises on strategy. A4: cron pulls the CSV monthly from the URL data.json currently points to (not hardcoded), and flags itself stale if data.json's 'modified' timestamp hasn't advanced past 40 days. A5: ingestion, alert dispatch, and Stripe dunning are all cron/webhook driven, fail-closed (alerts if ingestion job fails). A6: support is bounded to 'here is what CMS's own list says about this NPI' — no case handling, no phone-tag with MACs.
underlying.moat: Archiving every monthly CMS snapshot since launch lets the product infer a provider's next due date even while CMS still shows 'TBD' (by pattern-matching each NPI's historical 3-5 year revalidation cadence) — a genuine data asset a same-day scraper of the current file can't replicate.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: $79-249/mo tiered by NPIs monitored (25/100/500), undercutting the $780-per-event and $600-2,400/provider/year credentialing-firm alternative by an order of magnitude while running unattended.
underlying.revenue_model: Subscription SaaS, per-NPI-tier monthly billing via Stripe, annual discount.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: 3-4 weeks: CSV ingestion + NPI matcher + alert templating + Stripe checkout is the whole build.
underlying.risks: CMS could rename the dataset or change its schema (mitigated by resolving the download URL from data.json each run instead of hardcoding it); customers must keep their own NPI roster current or the match silently misses new hires; the six-month lookahead window means 'TBD' NPIs need the historical-pattern moat to be genuinely useful, not just cosmetic.
underlying.why_simple: One join key (NPI), one date-threshold alerting engine, one monthly cron — no generative judgment anywhere in the fulfilment path.

ballot.name: CarrierWatch
ballot.promise: The moment a carrier already in your approved network lapses on authority, insurance or UCR — or looks like a chameleon re-registration — you know before you tender the load.
ballot.synthesis: Standing monitor over FMCSA public files (L&I Socrata bulk datasets, QCMobile API, monthly SMS census) for a broker’s carrier list: insurance lapse, authority revocation/reinstation, new-authority red flags, shared-identity signals (address/phone/officer collisions with revoked carriers). Deterministic red-flag rules; no fraud “score” the model invents. Two mined ideas merged: continuity monitoring (lead tier) + point-in-time chameleon screen (onboarding tier).
ballot.buyer: Small freight brokerages and factoring shops under the price floor of SaferWatch/Carrier411; VerifyCarrier’s own tiering shows the long tail exists.

underlying.name: Carrier Continuity Watch
underlying.one_liner: A standing monitor (not a one-time lookup) that alerts freight brokers and factoring companies the moment a carrier already in their approved network lapses on UCR, BOC-3, or cargo/liability insurance — the negligent-hiring exposure that point-in-time vetting tools don't catch.
underlying.problem: Brokers get sued for negligent hiring/entrustment when a carrier they vetted months ago quietly lets its UCR registration, BOC-3 process-agent designation, or insurance lapse and then causes a loss — vetting at onboarding doesn't catch a mid-relationship lapse, which is exactly the ongoing-monitoring product category that firms like SaferWatch and CarrierOK sell as a distinct 'watchlist/monitoring' tier from their on-demand 'snapshot' search tier.
underlying.target_customer: Freight brokerages with an existing approved-carrier list (tens to low-hundreds of carriers) and factoring companies with a funded-carrier book, who need continuous rather than point-in-time compliance status.
underlying.evidence: The same incumbents that sell one-time carrier lookups also sell a separately-priced ongoing-monitoring product, proving the market treats 'watch this carrier over time' as distinct paid value: SaferWatch's own site distinguishes on-demand research from 'monitoring of your carrier watch list' within its $79.95/mo plan (fetched via search of https://truckbrokerinsurancenetwork.gtu-ins.com/why-we-and-you-should-use-saferwatch-for-carrier-selection/, 2026-08-19), and VerifyCarrier explicitly prices a separate 'Carrier Monitoring' product line ($49/$99/$249 per month for 50/250/unlimited monitored carriers with daily alerts on authority, insurance, and safety-rating changes) apart from its plain lookup API tiers (fetched https://verifycarrier.com/pricing, 2026-08-19). CarrierOK likewise runs a distinct no-contract monthly 'compliance' pricing page (https://www.carrier-ok.com/pricing?product=data, referenced via search 2026-08-19, page itself not yet directly fetched — flagged for confirmation before build).
underlying.knowledge_base: FMCSA Licensing & Insurance Socrata bulk datasets on data.transportation.gov — Active & Pending Insurance (qh9u-swkp) and Authority History (9mw4-x3tu), confirmed to exist via catalog.data.gov (fetched 2026-08-19) — for insurance-lapse and authority-status changes; the federal Unified Carrier Registration dataset on data.transportation.gov (fux9-ij6p), confirmed to exist via search of data.transportation.gov (fetched 2026-08-19, direct Socrata field/refresh-cadence confirmation still needed before build) for annual UCR compliance status; FMCSA QCMobile API for BOC-3/authority spot-checks between bulk refreshes (https://mobile.fmcsa.dot.gov/QCDevsite/docs/qcApi, fetched 2026-08-19). Staleness is detectable because Socrata datasets expose their own last-updated metadata and a failed/empty daily QCMobile spot-check flips a carrier to 'unconfirmed' rather than silently reporting old data.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: broker self-signs-up, uploads their existing approved-carrier CSV (DOT numbers), pays via Stripe — no sales call needed, mirroring how VerifyCarrier's monitoring tiers are self-checkout. A2: the alert is a deterministic diff between yesterday's and today's pulled government field values (authority status, insurance-on-file flag, UCR-current flag) — no human reviews the diff. A3: if a data source is unreachable that day, the affected carriers are marked 'not reconfirmed since [date]' rather than silently showing stale green status, and the product never asserts a status it can't currently source. A4: nightly cron diff against the Socrata bulk files plus QCMobile spot-checks, with dataset vintage timestamps driving automatic staleness flags. A5: ingestion, diffing, and alert dispatch are all cron jobs with fail-closed behavior (no 'all clear' email if the day's pull failed). A6: zero per-customer human minutes — the product's entire job is turning a public-data diff into an email/webhook.
underlying.moat: None beyond focus and price — same public data as Idea 1 and the same incumbent set (SaferWatch, VerifyCarrier, CarrierOK) already sell this as a line item, so the wedge is bundling it as a cheap always-on companion to Idea 1's onboarding check rather than a separately-sold enterprise module, undercutting the $79.95-$249/mo price points found.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: $39-$149/mo by number of monitored carriers (25/100/unlimited), positioned below SaferWatch's $79.95/mo all-in price and VerifyCarrier's $49-$249 monitoring tiers.
underlying.revenue_model: Recurring subscription tiered by watchlist size, self-serve Stripe billing.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: 3-5 weeks: slightly longer than Idea 1 because it depends on reliably parsing the UCR and Authority History bulk files rather than only the keyless QCMobile ad-hoc endpoint, so initial build time is a bit higher.
underlying.risks: The UCR dataset's exact API/Socrata field structure and refresh schedule were found to exist but not yet fetched and field-verified — must confirm before committing to build. This idea overlaps substantially with Idea 1's data pipeline and target customer, so it is best pitched as a companion add-on tier of the same product rather than a fully separate company, and a founder choosing between the three should treat Ideas 1 and 3 as one product with two pricing tiers if resources are constrained.
underlying.why_simple: Every alert is a before/after diff on structured government fields (authority-active boolean, insurance-on-file boolean, UCR-current boolean) — there is no generative judgment call about whether a carrier is 'compliant,' only a direct read of what the public record currently says.

underlying.name: Chameleon Carrier Screen
underlying.one_liner: Point-in-time fraud/identity screening API for freight brokers and factoring underwriters, built entirely from deterministic red-flag rules run against FMCSA's public carrier registration, insurance, and safety files.
underlying.problem: Before tendering a load or funding an invoice, brokers and factors must know whether a motor carrier is a legitimate, insured operator or a 'chameleon' carrier (freshly re-authorized after a revocation, insurance added days before pickup, address/officer overlap with a previously flagged MC number). The Transportation Intermediaries Association's fraud estimate and FMCSA's own complaint volume show this is a fast-growing, expensive problem, and multiple paid tools already exist to solve exactly this with public government data, none of them AI-generative — they run rules against SAFER/L&I fields.

underlying.name: MarkDocket

ballot.promise: Every weekly Medicare coverage update and quarterly NCCI edit drop, priced in dollars against the codes your practice actually bills — before it starts denying claims.

underlying.name: Denial Weather
underlying.one_liner: Reads every weekly Medicare coverage update and quarterly NCCI edit drop against the specific codes a practice actually bills, and puts a dollar figure and an effective date on each change before it starts denying claims.
underlying.problem: Medicare's coding and coverage rules change on a fixed, published, machine-readable schedule that almost no small practice can actually track. Local coverage documents refresh weekly (CMS ships MCD data sets every Thursday); NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits and Medically Unlikely Edits are republished quarterly, with individual edit files running to 475,091 records in the 2026 Q3 release; HCPCS Level II is quarterly; fee schedules are quarterly. When a claim hits a PTP edit, 'the Column One code is eligible for payment, but the Column Two code is denied unless a clinically appropriate NCCI PTP-associated modifier is also reported' — and an MUE denial is a coding denial, which means the practice cannot bill the patient for it either. So the loss is total and silent: the practice keeps billing the way it always has, discovers the change six weeks later in an EOB pile, and eats the rework and the write-offs. The incumbent tools (AAPC Codify and similar code-lookup subscriptions) are reference libraries: you must already know to go look. Nobody sells the inverse and personalized version — 'here are the 6 changes in this Thursday's drop that touch YOUR top 50 codes, in YOUR MAC jurisdiction, worth $41k against your last 90 days of volume, effective October 1.'
underlying.target_customer: 1-15 provider specialty practices with high code concentration and thin margins where a single edit change moves real money — physical and occupational therapy, behavioral health, dermatology, sleep, wound care, allergy/immunotherapy, independent labs and DME suppliers — plus the small third-party billing companies (5-100 client NPIs) that serve them and can resell the alerts.
underlying.revenue_model: Self-serve monthly subscription metered by number of watched HCPCS/CPT codes and NPIs, with a one-time quarterly impact report as the entry offer timed to the four annual edit drops (a natural, calendar-driven purchase trigger four times a year). Stripe self-serve, in-app tier changes, automated dunning. The billing-company tier is pure expansion revenue with no sales motion.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: One-time 'Quarterly Impact Report' $149 (upload a code+volume CSV, get a dated PDF of what the next drop does to you). Practice $99/mo (50 watched codes, one MAC, weekly LCD deltas). Group $299/mo (500 codes, multi-MAC, 835-derived volumes, dollar-impact modeling). Billing Company $799/mo (multi-NPI, white-labelled client digests, API). Anchor to a single avoided denial cohort: for a mid-size PT practice one changed MUE across a quarter is routinely five figures, so $299/mo prices at a few percent of one avoided event.
underlying.knowledge_base: (1) CMS Medicare Coverage Database downloads — current and retired LCDs, Articles and NCDs, shipped as .MDB and CSV with a Read Me and data dictionary, 'updated weekly on Thursdays' (the 08/02/2026 snapshot released 08/06/2026), plus the MCD Coverage API for programmatic access. (2) NCCI PTP and MUE quarterly ZIP files for practitioner, outpatient-hospital and DME supplier services. (3) HCPCS Level II quarterly updates. (4) MPFS RVU files, OPPS Addendum B, CLFS and the DMEPOS fee schedule. (5) MAC jurisdiction map (which contractor covers which state and which LCDs therefore bind). (6) CMS transmittals and MLN Matters articles. The proprietary layer is the longitudinal diff: CMS publishes snapshots, not changelogs, so a maintained revision history that answers 'what changed in this document, in this edit pair, in this MUE value, and when did it take effect' is assembly work nobody sells to small practices. Refresh cron: MCD download and diff every Thursday 20:00 ET plus a daily Coverage API poll for out-of-band NCD activity; NCCI/MUE poll daily during the two weeks around each quarterly release (Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct 1) and weekly otherwise; fee-schedule files monthly with pinned quarterly jobs; MAC map annually; transmittals weekly. Staleness detection: every source file is hashed; if the MCD weekly file hash is unchanged across two consecutive Thursdays, or a quarterly NCCI file arrives with a record count more than 10% off the prior quarter, the pipeline fails closed, suppresses that source's alerts, and shows a dated staleness banner with the last verified release date.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: signup, CSV upload, Stripe Checkout, and renewal all self-serve; the $149 impact report needs nothing but an email and a two-column CSV. A2: the change detection, the personalization against the customer's code list and volumes, the dollar math against their MAC's fee schedule, and the before/after policy diff are all generated; no coder reviews anything. A3: the honest failure mode is jurisdiction and applicability ambiguity — a code appears in a Billing and Coding Article but not the LCD, or the upload does not reveal place of service. The engine refuses to collapse that: it renders both outcomes with both dollar figures side by side ('applies only if your MAC is Noridian JE and POS is 11'), labels the item 'unresolved — 2 readings', quotes the governing paragraph verbatim with its document ID and version date, and lets the user set the disambiguating fact once in settings so it resolves permanently. It never asserts a modifier is 'clinically appropriate' — that is a clinical judgement and the product says so explicitly and links the CMS text instead. Items that stay unresolved are excluded from headline totals rather than folded in. No coder queue, no consult upsell, no 'contact us'. A4: six CMS sources, all machine-readable, on the crons above, with hash and record-count based staleness. A5: download, diff, personalize, send, bill, and monitor all scheduled; a source that fails validation blocks its own alerts rather than degrading silently. A6: zero human minutes; support is bounded because each alert carries the primary CMS document and the diff that produced it.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: 5-7 weeks. Week 1-2: MCD weekly ingestion plus the LCD/Article diff engine. Week 3: free public 'what changed in this week's Thursday drop' digest and per-code change-history pages (the SEO and email-list surface). Week 4: NCCI/MUE quarterly ingestion. Week 5: $149 impact report with CSV upload and checkout. Week 6-7: subscriptions and weekly personalized digests. Fastest revenue comes from timing launch to the two weeks before a quarterly edit effective date.
underlying.risks: (1) CPT code descriptors are AMA-licensed intellectual property — a hard, real constraint: the product must be built on CMS-published HCPCS and code numbers plus customer-supplied code lists, and must not redistribute CPT descriptor text without a license. This shapes the UI and needs deciding before a line of code. (2) PHI risk if users upload raw claim files; the product should accept only code + volume + MAC and reject anything patient-identifying at the parser, keeping it out of HIPAA scope by design. (3) Healthcare buyers are slow and often defer to their billing company; mitigation is making the billing-company tier the primary wedge, since one billing company brings dozens of NPIs. (4) Entrenched reference incumbents (AAPC Codify, Find-A-Code) could add personalization; mitigation is Dunford positioning — we are not a code lookup, we are a change-and-impact monitor, and the moat is the longitudinal diff history CMS does not publish. (5) Dollar-impact estimates depend on customer-supplied volumes and will be wrong if the upload is wrong; the product must show its arithmetic and label every figure as an estimate derived from the user's own file. (6) Federal fee-schedule policy shifts could reshuffle sources; mitigation is source-agnostic ingestion with per-source health checks.

underlying.name: SponsorScope
underlying.one_liner: A searchable, always-refreshed database of which U.S. employers actually filed H-1B/PERM sponsorship paperwork, at what wage, and how often — built entirely from DOL's own quarterly disclosure files — sold to recruiters and staffing agencies who need to know before they submit a candidate.
underlying.problem: Tech and healthcare recruiters routinely waste submittals pitching candidates who need visa sponsorship to employers that, per the public record, rarely or never file H-1B/PERM paperwork, or that file at wage levels far below what the recruiter is quoting. The government publishes the ground truth (every LCA and PERM filing, with employer, job title, wage and status) but only as raw quarterly spreadsheets with tens of millions of rows spanning 15+ years, not as a searchable product — which is exactly the gap that already-monetized third-party tools (a $199 'Sponsorship Premium' product on Gumroad, and free-to-freemium sites like MyVisaJobs and H1BGrader per search results) are built to fill.
underlying.target_customer: Tech/healthcare recruiting and staffing agencies, and RPO (recruitment process outsourcing) teams, who need employer-level sponsorship-history and wage-benchmark lookups before spending time on a submittal — priced as a per-seat or per-search SaaS tool, not a compliance product.
underlying.evidence: A live Gumroad product titled 'Sponsorship Premium' sells access to H-1B sponsorship data for $199 (confirmed by fetching https://maurobonfietti.gumroad.com/l/sponsor-premium on 2026-08-19, where the page's embedded pricing metadata reads `"price":199.0,"priceCurrency":"USD"`), demonstrating real money already changes hands for exactly this kind of employer-sponsorship lookup built on the same public LCA data. Search results independently surfaced MyVisaJobs and H1BGrader as established players in this same 'H-1B sponsor database' niche, indicating a durable market rather than a one-off product.
underlying.knowledge_base: DOL's Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC) Performance Data page publishes the full LCA (H-1B/H-1B1/E-3) and PERM disclosure files every fiscal quarter as structured Excel workbooks with documented record layouts, with history back to FY2008. Verified live on 2026-08-19: `curl` against https://www.dol.gov/media/LCA_Disclosure_Data_FY2026_Q3.xlsx returned HTTP 200, content-type `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet`, 251,850,891 bytes; the equivalent PERM file at https://www.dol.gov/media/PERM_Disclosure_Data_FY2026_Q3.xlsx returned HTTP 200, same content-type, 156,267,808 bytes. The OFLC performance index page (fetched https://www.dol.gov/agencies/eta/foreign-labor/performance, 2026-08-19) confirms this is a standing quarterly release with a documented record-layout PDF per file, so staleness is detectable by checking for the next fiscal-quarter file appearing on a fixed post-quarter-end schedule.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: self-serve account creation and Stripe checkout give immediate search/API access, no sales call. A2: fulfilment is a quarterly batch ETL (download the new disclosure file, normalize employer names/NAICS/wage fields, load into a search index) plus a deterministic query engine for the customer-facing lookups — no analyst reviews or edits a result before it's shown. A3: employer-name matching across years is fuzzy by nature (mergers, staffing-agency vs. end-client naming); rather than guessing, the product shows all plausible matches with a confidence indicator and the raw filing IDs so the user can disambiguate themselves, and returns 'no filings found in the public record' when there's genuinely no match instead of speculating. A4: a cron job checks for each program's next-quarter file on DOL's site on a schedule keyed to DOL's own quarterly release cadence, and the UI displays 'data current through FY2026 Q3, filed by DOL' so staleness is visible, not hidden. A5: ETL, indexing and billing are all schedulable and idempotent (safe to re-run), and fail closed by keeping serving the last-good quarter if a new file's schema doesn't validate. A6: the product's job is bounded to 'search public filings by employer/title/wage,' with no bespoke research, so support volume doesn't scale with customer count.
underlying.moat: The raw data is public and already has free/cheap competitors, so the moat is (a) 15+ years of schema-drifted quarterly files cleaned into one consistent, fast-searchable index, (b) employer-name deduplication/fuzzy-matching that raw spreadsheet users have to redo themselves every time, and (c) packaging and pricing specifically for the recruiter/staffing workflow (per-search or per-seat, integrable into an ATS) rather than the general-public lookup UX competitors ship today.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: $49-$149/mo per-seat for recruiter/staffing-agency search access (below the $199 one-time Gumroad anchor but recurring, reflecting continuous refresh value), with a metered API tier for ATS/CRM integrations priced per 1,000 lookups.
underlying.revenue_model: Monthly per-seat SaaS subscription plus a metered API add-on, billed via Stripe; no historical one-time sale needed since the value is the always-refreshed lookup, not a static export.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: Two to four weeks: the current-quarter file is already confirmed downloadable today, so the main lift before launch is the initial ETL/index build over the historical quarterly archive (a one-time batch job, not an ongoing dependency) plus the search UI.
underlying.risks: DOL's file schema and column names have drifted across fiscal years/quarters historically (visible in the range of filenames from FY2008 onward), so the ETL needs to tolerate schema changes without silently mis-mapping fields. The ~1-quarter publication lag means the product cannot claim 'real-time' sponsorship status, only 'most recent published filings' — must be stated clearly to avoid overpromising. The niche must stay strictly framed as 'historical sponsorship record + disclosed wage benchmarking' and never drift into computing or asserting a required prevailing-wage rate, which would cross into excluded territory. Free/cheap incumbents (MyVisaJobs, H1BGrader, the $199 Gumroad product) mean differentiation has to be real (recruiter workflow, API, seat pricing), not just 'we also have the data.'
underlying.why_simple: Every number shown (employer name, job title, filed wage, case status, filing count) is copied directly from DOL's own disclosure spreadsheet by deterministic ETL code; the only place any matching logic is applied is employer-name disambiguation, which is surfaced to the user as multiple ranked candidates rather than a single asserted answer, so no generative or judgment-based step ever produces the number a customer relies on.

underlying.name: PortfolioWatch UK
underlying.one_liner: Nightly diff-and-alert monitoring of Companies House filing deadlines and PSC/officer/status changes across a portfolio of hundreds of UK companies, for accountants and credit teams — built directly on the free, live Companies House API.
underlying.problem: Accountants managing many clients, and SME credit/collections teams tracking customers or suppliers, need to know the moment a company's confirmation statement or accounts go overdue, or its PSC/directors/status change (an early distress or change-of-control signal). Red Flag Alert, a paid monitoring tool for exactly this, starts at £200.00/month per Capterra's listing (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.capterra.co.uk/software/1044714/red-flag-alert) — direct evidence money already changes hands for portfolio-level company monitoring, at a price point far above what a small practice or SME credit team wants to pay for pure alerting.
underlying.target_customer: Small accountancy/company-secretarial practices (50-500 client companies) and SME finance/credit teams who need automated overdue-filing and ownership-change alerts across a book of UK companies, without a £200+/mo enterprise monitoring contract.
underlying.evidence: Red Flag Alert starting price £200.00 (Capterra UK, fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.capterra.co.uk/software/1044714/red-flag-alert). Adjacent evidence of willingness to pay for Companies-House-derived compliance tooling: Inform Direct's tiered company-secretarial pricing (fetched 2026-08-19, https://www.informdirect.co.uk/business-overview/pricing/) — £10/mo for the first company plus £0.69/company for companies 2-50, scaling down per company at higher volumes — shows practices already pay per-company recurring fees for Companies-House-linked deadline management (Inform Direct additionally files; a pure-monitoring product is a lighter, cheaper adjacent play).
underlying.knowledge_base: UK Companies House REST API, base https://api.company-information.service.gov.uk — verified LIVE by direct fetch on 2026-08-19 (unauthenticated request to /company/00000006 returned HTTP 401 'Empty Authorization header', confirming the endpoint is real and requires only a free API key, not a paid one). Rate limit confirmed via Companies House's own developer-specs rate-limiting guide (fetched 2026-08-19, https://developer-specs.company-information.service.gov.uk/guides/rateLimiting): 600 requests per 5-minute window, resetting automatically, with 429s on excess — a documented, generous, free ceiling. Company profile responses include structured confirmation_statement.next_due, accounts.next_due, and company_status fields; PSC endpoints return notified_on/ceased_on dates. Data updates same-day as filings; staleness is detectable by comparing a company's last-seen snapshot date against 'today'.
underlying.autonomy_case: A1: self-serve signup, add companies by number or CSV upload, Stripe billing — no onboarding call. A2: nightly cron polls the CH API per watched company, diffs the JSON against the prior snapshot, and emits deterministic alerts (accounts N days overdue, PSC added/removed, status changed to dissolved/liquidation) via a fixed template — no analyst touches any alert. A3: when a field is null (e.g., no accounts filed yet), the alert says 'not yet reported by Companies House' rather than inferring a risk score; the product never asserts a judgment the source data doesn't support. A4: the CH API is the live source of truth with no manual curation; a daily pipeline check flags staleness if no companies' snapshots have changed in an implausible window. A5: nightly ingestion cron, Stripe dunning, and uptime/health-check monitoring are all schedulable and fail-closed. A6: alerts are formulaic diffs — no bespoke integration or human risk review is offered, bounding support load by design.
underlying.moat: A time-series of each portfolio company's filing/PSC history becomes a proprietary baseline (e.g., 'this company is usually 3 days late, this time it's 90') that a one-off Companies House lookup can't replicate, and it compounds the longer a customer's portfolio is monitored.
underlying.pricing_hypothesis: $49-199/mo tiered by portfolio size (50/250/1,000 companies watched), undercutting Red Flag Alert's £200+/mo entry price for a narrower, monitoring-only feature set.
underlying.revenue_model: Monthly SaaS subscription tiered by number of monitored companies.
underlying.time_to_first_revenue: 2-3 weeks (CH API integration behind a free key, diff engine, Stripe, templated alert emails).
underlying.risks: Companies House itself may offer a free 'follow a company' single-company email alert (not yet verified live) which could blunt appetite for a paid tool at small scale — the wedge has to be portfolio scale (hundreds of companies), structured diffing, and historical baselining, not bare single-company alerts. Also, PSC register updates lag the underlying legal change by up to the statutory notification windows, which the product must state plainly rather than imply real-time.
underlying.why_simple: The paid deliverable is a JSON diff between two nightly API snapshots rendered into a template — no generative model is required to produce the alert content.
